findings.title: Sanitizer misses the `[1m]` suffix in the issue's real model value, so the model name keeps the suffix.
findings.body: The issue's example `llm_request` span has `"model": "claude-opus-4-6[1m]"`, which is Claude Code's marker for the 1M-context variant, not an ANSI escape. `ANSI_SGR_RE` needs an ESC byte, and `/\[[0-9;]*m$/` needs `m` to be the last character. Neither matches `[1m]`, which ends in `]`. So `gen_ai.request.model` becomes `claude-opus-4-6[1m]`. Model and pricing lookups keyed on the plain model id will likely not match it, so cost is lost. The test fixture uses an invented `claude-opus-4-6\u001b[1m` value, so it passes without covering the shape the issue shows. Strip a trailing `\[[^\]]*\]` context-variant suffix (or keep it in a separate attribute), and add a test with the literal `claude-opus-4-6[1m]` value.

findings.title: Any span with a `span.type` attribute now passes the default export filter.
findings.body: The new check returns true when the attribute key is `span.type`, whatever its value. `span.type` is a generic key that other libraries also set. Datadog-style bridges, for example, set it to `web`, `http`, `db` or `cache`. With this change, ordinary HTTP and DB spans that carry the key pass `isGenAiOrLlmAttributeSpan` and get exported by default. That defeats the smart filter this predicate exists for. The ingest side checks the value (`interaction` / `llm_request`) and the SDK should too. For example, read the attribute value and match only `interaction` or `llm_request`. `user_prompt` and `llm_request.context` are specific enough to keep as key matches.
